function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
Triangulation metrics are quantitative measures used to evaluate the accuracy, precision, and reliability of triangulation-based positioning or mapping systems. In a typical triangulation setup—such as GPS, surveying, or sensor networks—a set of known reference points (or “anchors”) is used to determine the location of unknown points by measuring angles or distances from multiple anchors.

Key aspects of triangulation metrics include:

| Metric | What it Measures | Typical Use |
|--------|------------------|-------------|
| **Horizontal/Vertical Dilution of Precision (HDOP/VDOP)** | The geometric spread of the reference points relative to the target. A lower DOP indicates better geometry and typically higher positional accuracy. | Used in GNSS receivers to estimate the expected error in horizontal or vertical coordinates. |
| **Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)** | The square root of the average squared difference between estimated positions and ground‑truth positions. | Commonly used to assess overall system performance over a dataset. |
| **Mean Absolute Error (MAE)** | The average absolute difference between estimated and true positions. | Provides a straightforward measure of average error magnitude. |
| **Standard Deviation / Variance** | The spread of errors around the mean. | Indicates consistency of the system; low variance means more reliable estimates. |
| **Bias / Systematic Error** | The average offset between estimated and true positions. | Detects systematic shifts due to calibration issues or environmental effects. |
| **Coverage Probability** | The proportion of estimates that fall within a specified error radius. | Useful for probabilistic assessment of system reliability. |
| **Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)** | The ratio of useful signal power to background noise. | Higher SNR generally leads to more accurate angle/distance measurements. |
| **Time to First Fix (TTFF)** | The time required to obtain the first valid position after powering on. | Important for applications requiring rapid initialization. |
| **Update Rate / Refresh Rate** | How often new position estimates are produced. | Determines how quickly the system can respond to changes in motion or environment. |

In practice, triangulation metrics are computed from raw measurement data (angles, distances, timestamps) and compared against known ground truth or high‑accuracy reference solutions. They help engineers:

1. **Diagnose problems** – e.g., a high HDOP may indicate poor anchor geometry or multipath interference.
2. **Validate system upgrades** – e.g., comparing RMSE before and after adding more anchors or improving algorithms.
3. **Set performance thresholds** – e.g., ensuring that 95 % of fixes lie within a 5 m radius for safety‑critical applications.

Understanding and monitoring these metrics is essential for maintaining the quality and trustworthiness of any triangulation‑based navigation or mapping solution.
